20.0.s.en: (1) The visit of Magdalene, Peter and John to the empty tomb

20.0.0.en: "The first day of the week": that is Sunday, the day of proclaiming victory and the breaking of the power of death. It became the Lord's Day in place of the Sabbath for all Christians from the first Church, in the apostolic age.

20.0.1.en: "When it was yet dark": how wonderful was Magdalene's love for the Lord! At the first threads of dawn, when the gates of Jerusalem were opened, she went out of the city to visit the tomb, while darkness still covered the western side completely... and she did not care that she was a woman... All she hoped for was to catch a glimpse of the tomb from the outside, but she saw the tomb empty, for the angel had rolled away the stone, as is mentioned in (Mt 28:2).

20.1.0.en: She hurried out as the first herald of the Resurrection, and her eagerness led her first to the house of Peter, the eldest and most renowned, and then to the house of John, where the Virgin Mary was staying. Since she did not yet grasp the dimensions of the Resurrection, she told them, according to what she had seen, that they had taken the Lord to an unknown place. The eagerness of Peter and John also appeared in their running toward the tomb, and John outran Peter because of his young age.

20.2.0.en: The body of the dead man was wrapped entirely in linen cloths, while his head was covered by a larger napkin that enclosed all of it, and it was a separate piece. The purpose of mentioning these details is to prove one thing, namely that the body was not stolen, because whoever wanted to steal the body would not have had time to unwind all these wrapped cloths, but would have taken the whole body and then thrown away the cloths somewhere far off.

20.2.1.en: St. John does not fail to mention some details in order to make us share the scene with him. His stooping down shows how low the door of the tomb was, and his not entering, after looking at the linen cloths, shows the awe of the moment. As for Peter's entering, it confirms his bold nature and readiness to act, which we have grown accustomed to.

20.3.0.en: Then John's courage came after Peter, and he entered too, and wonder turned into faith: faith in what Magdalene had told them, which he had doubted. It was a faith before which mind and tongue are powerless, faith that Christ had risen and come out by Himself from this dark tomb.

20.4.0.en: The death of Christ was a shock to the disciples because they had not understood the prophecies of the Old Testament about His resurrection... And this scene ends with the two disciples returning to Jerusalem, where their homes were.

20.5.s.en: (2) The appearance of the Lord Christ to Magdalene

20.5.0.en: The two disciples went back, but Mary's love bound her to the tomb, and she could not leave it. Instead she stooped down, because of the low door of the tomb, and looked inside, and saw two angels who appeared in the form of men. Mark described them as "a young man" (Mk 16:5), and Luke as "two men" (Lk 24:4), and St. John also makes clear the position in which they sat.

20.6.0.en: It is remarkable that Mary was not afraid of the presence of these two angels, who had not been there before.

20.6.1.en: "Woman, why weepest thou?": this question did not mean that they did not know the reason for her weeping, but rather that they disapproved of it, since one ought to rejoice at the resurrection of the Lord from the dead. Her answer came to express her lack of conviction, or let us say her lack of grasp of this Resurrection, for she still believed that the body had been taken away and did not know where it was.

20.6.2.en: And when she had finished her answer, "she turned herself back, and saw Jesus standing". And because she was in bewilderment and grief, she did not know who He was, for it was far from her imagination and expectation that this should be the person of the Lord Jesus.

20.7.0.en: The tomb was hewn in a rock within a garden, and so the quickest possibility that leapt to Magdalene's mind was that the one speaking, who was awake at this early hour of the morning, must be the gardener. She did not turn or look closely at His appearance or His voice, because the event of the Resurrection was not within our reckoning. As for Christ's question to her, it was of course not by way of inquiry, since He knows the thoughts of hearts, but to rouse her and to present Himself to her.

20.8.0.en: The Lord called her by her name, and her response was like that of the lamb that knows the voice of its shepherd, and she seemed to be waking from a dream and heedlessness to the wakefulness of the Resurrection, unable to believe, and she answered: "Rabboni", that is, Master, which was the expression and title by which Christ was addressed. Therefore, by this answer she declares to us her recognition of the person of Him who rose from the dead.

20.9.0.en: "Touch me not": in (Mt 28:9) we learn that Mary Magdalene and the other Mary held Him by the feet, so why did the Lord say here, "Touch me not"?

20.9.1.en: Some explain this situation by saying that Mary, the first time, did in fact touch Christ, but some doubts about the Resurrection returned to her, and for this reason Christ forbade her to touch Him, as a kind of spiritual discipline for her doubt of the Resurrection.

20.9.2.en: St. John Chrysostom, however, says that the Lord wanted to move Magdalene from a state of emotional attachment to His person to the truth of the Resurrection and the glory of His new divinity, as though He were leading her gradually to maturity, weaning her from fleshly feelings to higher spiritual ones.

20.9.3.en: There is also a third opinion, which holds that what Christ meant was: do not hinder Me or delay the proclamation of the Resurrection, for there is the work of informing the disciples that you must do, and then "for I am not yet ascended to my Father", that is, I am not ascending soon, but I will remain forty days, so this is not the only opportunity in which you will see Me. "My Father, and your Father": My Father in particular and your Father in general, that is, My hypostatic Father, whose Son I am, the Word, and your Father, that is, the general Fatherhood of God to all His believing children.

20.9.4.en: "My God, and your God": My God because the Father in His glory is greater than the Son incarnate on earth, whose glory is hidden, although the two are one; and your God because you are His creation.

20.10.0.en: So Magdalene hurried to tell the disciples that she had seen the risen Christ, and of all the conversation that took place between them, and that He would ascend to heaven after a period during which He would appear to them.

20.11.s.en: (3) The first appearance to the disciples

20.11.0.en: On the evening of Resurrection Sunday, St. John depicts the state of the ten disciples (since Judas had disappeared and Thomas was absent), their fear, and how the doors were tightly shut on them from the inside; yet this proves the doctrine of the glorified resurrection body, which is not subject to material laws.

20.11.1.en: The disciples were startled to find the Lord Christ in their midst, bestowing on them His divine peace to reassure their hearts and free them from the fear in which they had shut themselves.

20.11.2.en: So are we all... we have closed doors and high walls of fears or anxiety... and we all ask for Your peace and the shining of Your divine light upon us, that our hearts may be reassured and we may cast fear outside.

20.12.0.en: Christ gave proof of the resurrection of His body: He is therefore not a spirit or an apparition, but a risen body bearing the wounds of the Cross... And for this reason the disciples' joy was wonderful when they saw the Lord and were assured of His resurrection... and there is nothing in existence that equals the joy of seeing the Lord.

20.12.1.en: God has granted us to see Him with the eyes of faith in our daily life, a gift from which everyone who does not confess Him, or who lives outside His Church, has deprived himself. And this gift is a pledge for whoever abides in the love of God, that we shall see Him there in heaven and our joy in Him will be complete, a joy without care, grief, sighing or anxiety, as the Church prays in the Litany of the Departed.

20.13.0.en: Christ repeated the greeting of His peace, granted to them a second time, to increase their sense of reassurance, and then moved on to something else, namely the disciples' coming work. "As my Father hath sent me" for the work of redemption, which no one other than I can offer, "even so send I you" as preachers and witnesses of this redemption that has been accomplished.

20.14.0.en: "He breathed on them... the Holy Spirit": the Lord Christ had said earlier of the Holy Spirit that the Father would send Him in His name. And here He grants the disciples the gift of the Holy Spirit by breathing into their faces, because His authority is the authority of the Father Himself. We point out two things here:

20.14.1.en: That this breathing was the foundation of the sacrament of the priesthood in the New Testament.

20.14.2.en: That this breathing, in the apostolic tradition, became like the leaven which the Apostles received from the Lord Christ and deposited within the sacraments of the Church. The priest, in the sacrament of Baptism, also breathes into the face of the one baptized, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit." Likewise, in the sacrament of the priesthood the bishop breathes into the face of the priest and repeats the same words... and many priests also use it in the sacrament of confession as a breathing for the forgiveness of sins... and so on...

20.15.0.en: A verse that makes clear, without any ambiguity or doubt, the authority of the Holy Spirit present in the sacrament of the priesthood, which the Lord Christ granted in the preceding verse to His Apostles, who deposited it in the Church.

20.15.1.en: We content ourselves here with what St. Cyril the Great cited in explaining it: "Forgiveness belongs to the nature of God alone, but those to whom He has given His Holy Spirit He has granted to possess the power of forgiveness, because however they act, it is the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, through the sacrament of the priesthood, who forgives or retains sins. The work, however, is carried out by means of a man, the priest, and this authority derives from the Holy Spirit and not from the holiness of the man (see the incident of Peter with Sapphira and Ananias, Acts 5:1-10), and Peter's saying: 'Why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost?' (v. 3), and he did not say: to lie to me? As for the sacrament of the forgiveness of sins, repentance and confession, it is the acknowledgment before the Holy Spirit, who uses the hand of the priest to transfer the sins of the penitent to the account of the atoning blood of Christ. The Holy Spirit also declares, through the priest, God's forgiveness of this sin. For this reason the sacrament of confession is one of the most joyful and comforting sacraments for man, especially for the one who practices it with understanding and awareness.

20.16.0.en: Thomas represented the rationalist character that hinders simple faith of the heart, so that he refused to believe the rest of the pure Apostles and the testimony of the women of the Resurrection, and he also had a precedent (see ch. 14:5). Indeed he declared, in an unconcealed challenge, that he would not believe unless he saw and felt the wounds of the Cross materially. St. John mentions the attitude of the Apostle Thomas here because he considers it a prelude to the events of the coming appearance of Christ among His disciples.

20.17.s.en: (4) The second appearance to the disciples

20.17.0.en: On the following Sunday the appearance was repeated with the same circumstances, the only difference being the presence of Thomas, who had been absent before. After the Lord gave His peace to the disciples, He addressed His words directly to Thomas, and the aim of all of Christ's words is: "and be not faithless, but believing".

20.17.1.en: Christ's manner with Thomas gives us an example of largeness of heart, kindness and long-suffering, even toward one who doubted and made it a condition for God to answer his requests before he would believe in His resurrection, to teach us thereby the true meaning of humility, condescension and compassion for people in their spiritual weaknesses.

20.17.2.en: Some also hold that Christ's words were not without gentle reproach.

20.18.0.en: "My Lord and my God": Thomas's answer came as "a declaration and an apology": a strong declaration of faith, and also an apology for his shame at Christ's gentle reproach for his blatant unbelief. Thomas did not say only "My Lord", but also "and my God", a strong expression by which he conveys his understanding of the mystery of the Resurrection, and that he was before the incarnate God, who by His divinity broke the sting and power of death.

20.19.0.en: Here the Lord Christ also gently reproaches Thomas for his doubt, for it was not fitting for a disciple who had lived with Christ more than three years, in which he saw the miracles and heard the teachings, to take such a position, demanding a material sight of the risen Christ. And for this reason the Lord Christ also declares the blessedness, that is, the blessings, which everyone who believes in Him receives in every age, without letting his mind stand as an obstacle to his faith.

20.20.0.en: St. John makes clear here the purpose of writing his whole Gospel: that it was not a book to enumerate the miracles and wonders, which all the books of the world could not contain (ch. 21:25), but it had one purpose only, which is the faith that Jesus the man is the Christ, God, and is the hypostasis of the Word, the eternal and heavenly Son of God. It is as though John, as he concludes his Gospel, reminds us of what he had already declared about the person of the Lord Christ in his first chapter, that the Word is the Son of God and that the Word was God, and he gives all readers the summary of his whole Gospel and its purpose, namely that there is no life and no eternity outside the name of Christ; for those who received Him are the only ones who became children of God.

20.20.1.en: Our beloved God, grant us this living and active faith which is the secret of overcoming the world, as St. John said in his first epistle: "Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God?" (1 Jn 5:5).

20.20.2.en: The appearance of Christ to the disciples a second time and His last commission to Peter to shepherd the flock

21.0.0.en: The Sea of Tiberias is the same as the Sea of Galilee, but St. John attributes it to the modern city of Tiberias, which was built by Herod, who was tetrarch of Galilee. The number of the disciples was seven, among them John and his brother James, and two of the disciples who were not of the Apostles.

21.0.1.en: "After these things Jesus shewed himself again": a phrase that points to the multiplicity of the appearances of the Resurrection after the previous appearances, to prove the divinity of the Lord Christ, as will become clear from the kind of this miracle.

21.1.0.en: Some thought that what Peter did was a turning back to the world, while others thought there was nothing in this, for Christianity did not forbid work; rather this was a course proclaimed by St. Paul in (Acts 20:34; 1 Thess 3:8).

21.1.1.en: The most moderate of these opinions is what St. Gregory the Great said: "Peter returned to fishing, but not to collecting taxes, because there are occupations to which one cannot return after renewal." It can also be said that what is held against Peter is his return to his first occupation without accompanying it with any work of preaching.

21.2.0.en: After they had toiled and failed to catch anything, the appearance of the Lord occurred, obscure at its beginning, and the dawn with its faint light removed its obscurity. The Lord Christ addressed them with His question: "Have ye any meat?" that is, anything to eat with bread, and the intended meaning of course is fish. Their negative reply expressed their condition. And of course the Lord's question here was only a preparation for the coming miracle.

21.3.0.en: The Lord offers advice to the fishermen, the servants, who were exhausted and had labored all night, reminding us of the first advice by which Peter recognized the Lord Christ in (Lk 5:4). It can be said that this miracle is a lesson for what happens in our life every day, and in the life of servants in particular, for we often depend on our hearts, our understanding and our experiences without God, whereas dependence on God and His word is behind true success; there is no value in any effort separated from God who works in His Church... and no value in any work that Christ does not bless, as if Christ were giving the disciples and the Church this lesson so that we may act on it in every aspect of our life. Peter, who followed Christ, denied Him when he depended on himself, despite his love for Him. But when the Holy Spirit worked in him, on the day of Pentecost he caught with his sermon 3,000 souls (Acts 2:41). Was that not a great deal of fish...?!

21.4.0.en: "He was naked": because they were fishing, Peter had taken off everything that hindered him in his work, and John, with his loving heart and greater alertness, was quick in faith to grasp what was happening and to connect the events with one another. For this reason his declaration was strong, firm and joyful: "It is the Lord."

21.4.1.en: Although it would have been natural for Peter to throw himself in as he was, he did something unnatural: he put on what he had taken off before throwing himself into the water. And we may understand that what Peter did:

21.4.2.en: First: befits the honor of God, before whom the angels cover their feet and their faces.

21.4.3.en: Second: relates to Peter himself, for he still felt shame because of the sin of his denial, as though he were covering not only his body but his naked soul, which, although it had wept bitterly, had not yet heard from the Lord His forgiveness of it.

21.5.0.en: The distance between the boat and the shore was about 95 meters, and what matters more is the spiritual, contemplative meaning here: the boat is the Church, the disciples are its priests and servants, and the fish are the souls that the Church has drawn from drowning in the world to the shore of spiritual deliverance...

21.5.1.en: And when everyone who has labored in service and drawn souls to God comes out, he finds that the almighty Christ has prepared for him food and a heavenly portion, as though He were rewarding with a special reward everyone who has toiled and kept vigil in catching souls for Him.

21.5.2.en: "Bring... which ye have now caught": ... we notice two things:

21.5.3.en: First: that what the disciples caught was fundamentally a miracle worked by the Lord, yet God, in His humility, attributes His work to His children...

21.5.4.en: Second: that He wants them to bring from their nets, in addition to what He Himself had prepared for them, in order to share the table with them and in their joy.

21.5.5.en: And this teaches us something important, which is that God is the One who works. But man too must offer to God what he has of energy, effort and money, so that the limited and weak is united with the work of God of infinite power.

21.6.0.en: The fish were very large and abundant (153), a number beyond imagination to come out in a single haul. It means that despite the darkness of the world and the multitude of spiritual battles, the Church of Christ, by the power of His work, is able to draw many and great souls, because she comes with all her abilities and gifts to the Kingdom, however long and pitch-dark the night (the darkness of the world) may be.

21.6.1.en: "Come and dine": God is the source of all nourishment. Did He not feed the people before in the wilderness, and likewise in the miracle of feeding the multitudes? He is the source of satisfaction for all who follow Him, satisfying them in every respect... spiritually and materially.

21.6.2.en: "None of the disciples durst ask": ... this points to the awe of the Person and the awe of the situation itself. And St. John gives another reason for their not asking Him, namely their knowledge and certainty that He was the Lord Jesus, as though the situation did not call for a question. Perhaps their caution and awe at this situation kept them standing, despite the Lord's invitation to them to eat, so the Lord Christ Himself came forward and took the bread and the fish, completing the course of His humility. For He, God and Lord, offers and performs the duty of hospitality for His disciples... And of course, when St. John said "This is now the third time", he did not mean by this that it was the last time, but it is a sequential record of what he had reported in the previous appearances.

21.7.0.en: After the meal Christ directed His words to Peter, but He called him by his human name and not the name He had given him as an apostle, since by his denial he had come down to the level of an ordinary man: "lovest thou me more than these?"

21.7.1.en: And here Peter recalls what he had said earlier in pride, setting himself apart from the rest of the Apostles (see Mt 26:33; Mk 14:29), and he answered: "Thou knowest that I love thee." Christ's comment was a charge to Peter that the proof of true love is the shepherding of the sheep, that is, souls or the Church, for the love of the faithful servant for his master is the shepherding of his children with all faithfulness, devotion and self-giving, and not by words or by claiming this love, which may fail before trials because of our false claim, as happened first with Peter.

21.8.0.en: The Lord Christ repeats the question twice after the first, to answer Peter's three denials. And each time He commands him that the true apology which He accepts from him is the shepherding of His people. However, the third time St. John shows us Peter's grief at the repetition of the question, so he wanted to defend himself against the charge of not loving Christ, and said to Him: "Thou knowest", that is, You do not need my answer to the question, for You are the searcher of hearts and know what is within them... and You also know that, if I denied You, it was out of human weakness.

21.9.0.en: What Christ said here to Peter directly applies to all of us indirectly in its spiritual meaning. For man in his spiritual youth, with little experience of faith, depends on himself and on his own human arms in service and in his life in general. But when he grows and increases in experience in the spiritual life, he becomes more humble and obedient to the work of the Holy Spirit, so the human self disappears and in its place comes a life of complete surrender to the divine will and purpose. As for the direct meaning for Peter, which St. John made clear in (v. 18): you, Peter, in the youth of your faith were impetuous, and promised what you could not do. But when you grow, you will go forward, by the power of the Holy Spirit working in you, to the death that frightened you before, and you will accept crucifixion head downward, and the end of your life and your martyrdom will be the greatest glorification you offer to My holy name.

21.9.1.en: And we all, how greatly we need, O God, to rely on the work of Your Holy Spirit in our life, emptying ourselves and stretching out our arms, that You alone may take the lead by Your good will; as for our own thinking, it is utterly deficient.

21.10.0.en: The last word Christ said to Peter was: "Follow me." After Peter was reassured of his return to his apostolic standing, and of Christ's forgiveness of the sin of his denial of Him, he turned to St. John, whom he saw also following Christ, and turned to Christ asking about John's future fate, which was a question out of place, since Peter gave himself a right that was not his, to ask about the standing or future of another, which is a matter belonging to the very work and will of God. For this reason the answer of the Lord Christ to Peter was decisive: "what is that to thee?" It means that this is none of your concern... attend to the matter that I direct to you alone, which is that you follow Me, without looking to anyone else, even if I wish him to remain alive until My second coming.

21.10.1.en: Perhaps the answer of the Lord Christ to Peter is an answer directed to all of us, for our thoughts often slip into comparisons or inquiries that are none of our business, such as asking whether others will be saved or not, and Christ's answer to us is: "Follow thou me... and you have no concern with others." May we take in these words, and not be occupied with anything but the salvation of our own souls...

21.11.0.en: He clarifies the confusion that arose in the disciples' understanding of Christ's last saying, and St. John explained it.

21.12.0.en: Here, as St. John has come to the end of his Gospel, it was important to him to emphasize two things:

21.12.1.en: First: the truth of his testimony, because he saw and wrote with his own hand what he witnessed, and not by report from another.

21.12.2.en: Second: that what he mentioned in his Gospel and his testimony is not everything, for he mentioned some things for the sake of faith in the person of the Lord Christ, and not an enumeration of all His miracles, discourses or parables, as the other Gospels attempted, though they mentioned only a little, as much as they could. And he shows the greatness of what the Lord did, and the impossibility of recording everything, in a beautiful turn of phrase, saying that all the books of the world are not enough to write down everything about the Lord Jesus; indeed, the world itself, in all its breadth, could not contain these books. And to our God be glory forever... Amen.
